title: Finiteness of automaton semigroups
formal: Historical question, resolved negatively: is there one deterministic algorithm which, given any finite complete deterministic Mealy automaton \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,\lambda)\), always halts and decides whether its generated transformation semigroup \[S(\mathcal A)=\{T_{q_m}\circ\cdots\circ T_{q_1}:m\ge1,\ q_1,\ldots,q_m\in Q\}\] is finite? Here all transformations act on all finite words \(\Sigma^*\). Gillibert's Theorem 3.13 proves that no such algorithm exists for this unrestricted input class.

source_formulation.text: Is finiteness decidable for the semigroup generated by an arbitrary finite complete Mealy automaton?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the 2013 general question, subsequently resolved

why: A small finite machine can describe infinitely many distinct transformations under composition. The question asks whether that unbounded algebraic behavior can nevertheless be recognized effectively from the machine table. Its negative resolution establishes a basic limit on structural algorithms for automaton semigroups, despite decidable equality of two explicitly represented elements and strong algorithms in restricted classes.
status_note: Resolved negatively by Gillibert, International Journal of Algebra and Computation 24(1), 2014, DOI 10.1142/S0218196714500015; checked author v2 Theorem 3.13. The proof constructs finite complete deterministic Mealy automata, matching the general question in Klimann 2013. The 2024 freeness paper confirms the result as known. No Lean formalization was checked.

importance.reason: A foundational undecidability boundary for algebraic structures generated by finite transducers, with a checked general negative theorem resolving the imported source question.

sentences: Each state of a finite Mealy machine defines a transformation of all finite input words.
Composing these state transformations generates a semigroup that may contain infinitely many distinct elements.
The historical question asks whether one always-terminating algorithm can decide finiteness from an arbitrary complete machine table.
Gillibert proved the answer negative in a result published in 2014, matching the unrestricted semigroup model.
The card is archived as resolved, while positive algorithms for restricted reversible or invertible machines remain separate results.

definitions:
The state set \(Q\) and input/output alphabet \(\Sigma\) are finite and nonempty, with cardinalities supplied as part of the input. A complete deterministic Mealy automaton has total maps \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) and \(\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Sigma\). At state \(q\), reading the letter \(a\) outputs exactly the letter \(\lambda(q,a)\) and changes state to \(\delta(q,a)\). There are no initial or accepting states; every state supplies a generator. The input consists of the full transition and output tables, using binary indices for states and letters. No invertibility, reversibility, state-number bound or alphabet-size bound is promised.

Write \(\varepsilon\) for the empty word and \(aw\) for a letter followed by a finite word. Each state induces a length-preserving, prefix-preserving total function defined recursively by \(T_q(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and \(T_q(aw)=\lambda(q,a)T_{\delta(q,a)}(w)\). The semigroup operation is function composition on \(\Sigma^*\). Two compositions represent the same element exactly if they agree on every finite input word of every length. The nonempty composition convention does not automatically adjoin an identity; an identity may already be a product of state functions. Adjoining one changes the cardinality by at most one and does not change finiteness.

Finiteness means there are only finitely many distinct functions in \(S(\mathcal A)\), rather than finitely many states, finitely many reachable states in the underlying graph, or finitely many actions on one fixed word length. Equivalently, some integer \(N\) and \(N\) nonempty state words represent every product transformation. The algorithm sought in the historical question is a single ordinary Turing machine, uniform over all finite tables. It returns exact YES/NO answers and halts on both finite and infinite instances. There is no prescribed time bound, random error, oracle, approximation or fixed maximum word length to inspect. Malformed finite tables may be rejected.
answer_criterion: For the archived negative resolution, a complete Lean formalization must define the finite Mealy-table encoding, induced transformations on all finite words, semantic equality, generated semigroup and total computability, and prove that no total computable predicate decides finiteness on every valid input. An acceptable formalized reduction must verify that every constructed table is finite, complete and deterministic and establish both directions of the source-problem correspondence. Undecidability only for partial or asynchronous transducers would not by itself match this statement. The cited published theorem is a mathematical resolution; this editorial review does not claim an existing Lean verification or supply one.

context_blocks.text: The finite state set describes generators, not all generated transformations. A product of states acts on words of arbitrary length, so the semigroup can be infinite even though the machine table is finite.

Klimann’s 2013 paper records general finiteness as open while proving a finite-or-free dichotomy for reversible two-state machines and decision results with additional invertibility. Here invertible means each state’s output map on letters is a permutation; reversible means each letter’s transition map on states is a permutation. Those are substantive restrictions absent from this general target.

Gillibert subsequently proves undecidability for precisely finite complete Mealy automata. The checked construction uses total transition/output maps, so its theorem does not depend on allowing undefined transitions or outputs of variable length.

The negative proof connects the existence of a plane tiling for a finite north-west-deterministic Wang tile set to infiniteness of the generated semigroup. The full paper, Lemmas 3.11–3.12 and Theorem 3.13, fixes the direction: a valid tiling corresponds to an infinite semigroup. The arXiv landing-page abstract has the opposite word in this correspondence, so the resolution was checked against the actual theorem and lemmas.

Equality of two specified state products and finiteness of the entire generated semigroup are different decision problems. The source records the former as decidable; that does not provide a computable bound on how many distinct products the latter may require.

The MFCS 2024 paper independently records the finiteness result as known while studying freeness. This confirms that retaining the 2013 source question as currently open would be incorrect. No conclusion about the group freeness question is inferred from semigroup finiteness.
